lesson.title: Triggering: Making a Repeating Signal Stand Still
lesson.summary: Triggering is the oscilloscope function that starts each new horizontal sweep at the same repeating feature of the input signal, such as a rising edge crossing a chosen voltage level, so that successive sweeps overlay each other and the waveform appears as a stable image instead of a scrolling blur.
lesson.body:
An oscilloscope does not draw a waveform once and leave it on screen; it continuously redraws, sweeping the trace from left to right over and over, many times per second. If each new sweep simply started as soon as the previous one finished, with no regard for where the input signal happened to be in its cycle at that instant, each redraw would begin at a slightly different point in the waveform, and the displayed image would appear to drift sideways or dissolve into an unreadable blur. Triggering is the mechanism that prevents this by choosing, deliberately, when each sweep is allowed to begin.

A trigger circuit watches an incoming signal, usually the same signal being displayed, though it can be set to watch a different channel or an external input, and waits for that signal to cross a specific voltage, the trigger level, moving in a specific direction, the trigger slope, either rising or falling. Only when that exact condition occurs does the scope start a new sweep. Because the same feature of the waveform, say, a rising edge crossing 0 volts, initiates every single sweep, each new trace lines up perfectly on top of the last one, and the eye perceives a single, motionless picture rather than a rapid series of slightly different, overlapping ones.

Take the 100 Hz sine wave from earlier examples, with a period of 10 ms. Set the trigger level to 0 volts and the slope to rising, and the scope waits, every cycle, for the signal to cross zero on its way up, then begins that sweep from that exact instant. The result is a rock steady image of the waveform. Now imagine the trigger level is set above the sine wave's actual peak amplitude, a voltage the signal never reaches. The trigger condition is never satisfied, the scope has no repeating event to lock onto, and it either free runs on its own timing, producing a scrolling, unstable image, or shows nothing useful at all, depending on the scope's trigger mode. Choosing a trigger level that actually falls within the signal's amplitude range is therefore not a minor detail, it is what makes the display usable in the first place.

This same mechanism is exactly what makes the dual channel phase measurement from earlier possible. When you compare two signals on a scope to find their phase difference, the trigger locks the sweep to one of them, and because both channels are drawn against that same synchronized time axis, the second channel's waveform holds a fixed, measurable position relative to the first, sweep after sweep, rather than drifting relative to it. Without reliable triggering, there would be no stable time shift to measure at all.
